recipes.name: Gulyásleves (Hungarian goulash soup)
recipes.description: The herdsmen's soup of the Hungarian plains: beef simmered slowly with onions, sweet paprika and caraway, then filled out with root vegetables, potatoes and tiny pinched noodles (csipetke).
equipment: Large heavy pot (at least 5 litres) with a lid

ingredients.name: Hungarian wax pepper or green bell pepper
Hot cherry pepper or fresh red chilli

steps.t: Heat the oil in the large pot over medium heat. Add the onions and cook gently, stirring now and then, until soft, translucent and just turning golden at the edges, 8–10 minutes. Don't rush this: the sweetness of the onions is the base of the soup.

Add the beef, turn the heat up to medium-high and stir until the cubes have lost their raw red colour on all sides, about 5 minutes. They will release liquid; that is fine, goulash is not seared hard like a French stew.

Take the pot off the heat and stir in the paprika, caraway and garlic. Paprika burns and turns bitter in seconds over a flame, so stir for 30 seconds off the heat until the meat is coated brick-red, then pour in 250 ml of the water straight away.

Return the pot to low heat, cover and braise the beef in this small amount of liquid for 1 hour, stirring every 15 minutes and adding a splash more water whenever it runs low. The meat should simmer gently in a thick, red, onion-paprika sauce.
Add the carrots, parsley root, tomato, pepper and the rest of the water. Bring back to a simmer, season with the salt and some pepper and cook, partly covered, for 20 minutes.

Meanwhile make the csipetke: mix the flour, egg and pinch of salt into a stiff, dry dough, kneading for 2–3 minutes until smooth (add a few drops of water only if it will not come together). Flatten it to about 5 mm and pinch off pea-sized pieces with floured fingers onto a floured plate.

Add the potatoes to the soup and simmer for 15 minutes, until almost tender. Drop in the csipetke and cook for 8–10 minutes more, until the noodles float, are cooked through when you bite one and the beef is tender enough to cut with a spoon.

Taste and adjust the salt; the broth should be rich, red and slightly peppery. Ladle into deep bowls and serve with fresh white bread and the hot pepper on the side for anyone who likes heat. Like most stews, goulash is even better the next day.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: In Hungary gulyás is a soup; the thick stew most people outside Hungary call goulash is closer to pörkölt.
Freezes well for up to 3 months without the potatoes and noodles; add those when you reheat.

recipes.name: Csirkepaprikás (chicken paprikash) with nokedli
recipes.description: Chicken braised in a velvety sauce of slow-cooked onions, sweet paprika and sour cream, served with nokedli, Hungary's soft little egg dumplings.
equipment: Wide heavy casserole with a lid
Spätzle maker or colander with large holes

ingredients.name: Chicken legs and thighs, bone-in, skin removed
Hungarian wax pepper or green bell pepper
Salt
ingredients.prep: plus more for the cooking water

steps.t: Heat the oil in the casserole over medium heat and add the onions with a pinch of salt. Cook slowly, stirring often, until very soft and pale gold, 12–15 minutes. They should melt into the sauce later, so keep the heat moderate and stop before they brown.
Add the chicken pieces and turn them in the onions over medium-high heat for about 5 minutes, until the surface turns white all over.

Pull the pan off the heat and stir in the paprika for 30 seconds so it colours the oil and coats the chicken without scorching (burnt paprika is bitter). Immediately add the pepper, tomato, water and salt and return to the heat.

Bring to a simmer, cover and cook gently for 30–35 minutes, turning the pieces once, until the chicken is tender and the juices run clear when the thickest thigh is pierced next to the bone (74 °C on a thermometer).

While the chicken cooks, make the nokedli batter: beat the flour, eggs, water and salt with a wooden spoon for 2–3 minutes into a thick, sticky, elastic batter that falls slowly from the spoon. Bring a large pan of well-salted water to a rolling boil.

Press the batter through the spätzle maker (or scrape it through the holes of a colander with a spatula) straight into the boiling water in two batches. Stir once; the dumplings are done 1–2 minutes after they rise to the surface. Lift them out with a slotted spoon, drain and toss with the butter.
Whisk the sour cream with the tablespoon of flour until smooth, then whisk in 3–4 tablespoons of the hot cooking liquid to temper it, so it warms gradually and does not curdle when it meets the pan.

Lift the chicken onto a plate, stir the sour cream mixture into the sauce and simmer gently for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until it thickens to a glossy, coral-pink sauce. Return the chicken, warm through without boiling hard, and taste for salt.
Serve the chicken and plenty of sauce over the nokedli, with a cucumber salad dressed with vinegar on the side.

recipes.reheating: Reheat gently, covered, over low heat with a splash of water until steaming hot (74 °C); boiling hard can split the sour cream.
notes: Hungarian cooks often use bone-in chicken legs with the skin on; this version removes the skin for a lighter sauce.

recipes.name: Lángos (fried flatbread with sour cream and cheese)
recipes.description: Hungary's favourite market and beach snack: soft yeasted dough stretched thin, fried until puffed and golden, brushed with garlic water and heaped with sour cream and grated cheese.
equipment: Deep frying pan or wide pot

ingredients.name: Oil
ingredients.prep: plus a little for your hands

ingredients.name: Grated cheese (trappista, Edam or mild cheddar)

steps.t: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt in the bowl, then pour in the milk, water and tablespoon of oil. Stir into a soft, slightly sticky dough and knead on the worktop for 8–10 minutes, until it is smooth and elastic and springs back when you poke it.
Return the dough to the oiled bowl, cover and leave somewhere warm for about an hour, until doubled in size. Meanwhile stir the crushed garlic into the 3 tablespoons of water and leave it to infuse.
Divide the dough into 6 pieces and shape each into a ball. Cover and rest for 10 minutes so the gluten relaxes and the dough stretches without tearing.

Heat the frying oil in the pan to 180 °C (a cube of bread should brown in about 40 seconds). With oiled hands, stretch each ball into a round about 18 cm across, thinner in the middle with a slightly thicker rim, like a small pizza.

Lower one lángos carefully into the oil, laying it away from you so it does not splash. Fry for about 1½ minutes per side, until puffed and deep golden, spooning hot oil over the top so it blisters. Drain on the rack and fry the rest one at a time, letting the oil come back to temperature in between.

While each lángos is still hot, brush it with the garlic water, spread with a thick layer of sour cream and scatter with grated cheese and a little dill. Eat at once, folded in half, while the edges are still crisp.

recipes.storage: Best eaten freshly fried. Plain, untopped lángos keep for 1 day wrapped at room temperature.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp plain lángos in a 200 °C oven for 4–5 minutes, then add the toppings.
notes: Some cooks add 100 g of cold mashed potato to the dough for an even softer centre.

recipes.name: Chicken schnitzel, Viennese style (Hühnerschnitzel Wiener Art)
recipes.description: Thin chicken escalopes coated in flour, egg and fine breadcrumbs and fried in plenty of hot fat until the crumb puffs into golden waves. Served with lemon and potato salad.
equipment: Cling film or a freezer bag

steps.t: Lay each butterflied breast between two sheets of cling film and pound it gently with the rolling pin, working from the centre outwards, until it is an even 4–5 mm thick. Even thickness is the secret: thin escalopes cook through in the time it takes the crumb to brown.
Season the escalopes on both sides with salt and white pepper. Set out three plates: flour in the first, the eggs beaten with the milk in the second, and breadcrumbs in the third.

Coat each escalope in flour and shake off the excess, then draw it through the egg so it is covered all over and let the surplus drip off. Finally lay it in the breadcrumbs and pat them on lightly without pressing; a loose coat is what lets the crumb puff away from the meat. Bread the schnitzels just before frying so the coating stays dry.
Heat the oil in the frying pan to about 170 °C, about 1.5 cm deep; a breadcrumb dropped in should sizzle immediately. Fry two schnitzels at a time so the fat stays hot.

Fry for 2–3 minutes per side, constantly shaking the pan gently and spooning hot fat over the top, until the crumb has puffed into golden ripples. Turn once with tongs. The chicken is done when the thickest part is white all the way through and reaches 74 °C.

Lift the schnitzels onto kitchen paper for a few seconds to drain, then fry the second batch. Serve immediately with lemon wedges, a sprinkle of parsley and Swabian potato salad, buttered parsley potatoes or a green salad.

recipes.reheating: Re-crisp on a rack in a 200 °C oven for 8–10 minutes until steaming hot; the microwave makes the crumb soggy.
notes: A true Wiener Schnitzel is made with veal; chicken or turkey versions are labelled 'Wiener Art' (Viennese style) in Austria.

recipes.name: Käsespätzle (cheese spätzle with crispy onions)
recipes.description: Fresh egg spätzle layered with melting Alpine cheese and topped with butter-fried onions: the Swabian and Allgäu answer to macaroni cheese.
equipment: Spätzle press, spätzle board or colander

ingredients.name: Salt
ingredients.prep: plus more for the cooking water

steps.t: Beat the flour, eggs, water, salt and nutmeg with a wooden spoon for 3–5 minutes until the batter is thick, smooth and full of air bubbles, and stretches in sheets when you lift the spoon. Let it rest for 10 minutes while the water heats.

Melt the butter in the frying pan over medium heat and add the onions. Fry, stirring often, for 15–20 minutes until deep golden brown and crisp at the edges. Lift onto kitchen paper; keep the buttery pan. Heat the oven to 180 °C.

Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil and salt it well. Press a third of the batter through the spätzle press into the water (or scrape thin strips off a wet board with a knife). Once the spätzle rise to the surface, cook for 30 seconds more, then lift them out with a slotted spoon.

Shake the spätzle briefly to drain them, then layer straight into the ovenproof dish with a third of the cheese and a grind of pepper, so the heat of the noodles starts the cheese melting. Repeat with the rest of the batter and cheese in two more batches.
Toss the last layer in the onion pan to pick up the browned butter, then put the dish in the oven for 8–10 minutes, until all the cheese is melted and stretchy and the top just starts to bubble.
Pile the crispy onions on top, scatter with chives and serve at once with a green salad dressed with vinegar, or a potato and cucumber salad, to cut the richness.

recipes.reheating: Reheat in a covered pan with a splash of milk over low heat, or in a 180 °C oven, until steaming hot.
notes: Spätzle batter should be thicker than pancake batter; if it runs off the spoon, add a spoonful of flour.

recipes.name: Rösti (Swiss potato cake)
recipes.description: Coarsely grated, parboiled potatoes pressed into a pan and fried slowly in butter until a thick golden crust forms on both sides. The classic partner to Zürcher Geschnetzeltes or a fried egg.
equipment: Non-stick or well-seasoned frying pan (about 26 cm)

ingredients.name: Waxy or all-purpose potatoes
ingredients.prep: boiled in their skins the day before and chilled

steps.t: Peel the cold, cooked potatoes (the skins slip off easily) and grate them on the coarse side of the grater into long strands. Season with the salt and a little pepper and toss gently with your fingers so the strands stay separate.

Heat half the butter with the oil in the frying pan over medium heat until foaming. Add the potatoes, spread them out and press lightly with a spatula into an even cake about 2 cm thick, tidying the edges.

Fry for 10–12 minutes without stirring, shaking the pan now and then, until the underside has a thick golden-brown crust. Lift an edge with the spatula to check; if it is browning too fast, turn the heat down.
Slide the rösti out onto the plate, cover with the upturned pan and flip it back in, browned side up. Add the remaining butter around the edge so it runs underneath.
Fry the second side for 8–10 minutes until equally crisp and golden. Slide onto a board, cut into wedges and serve hot, as a side or topped with a fried egg for a simple supper.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh. Leftovers keep in the fridge, covered, for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 3–4 minutes per side until hot through.
notes: Cooking the potatoes a day ahead lets the starch set, so the strands hold together without egg or flour.

recipes.name: Rinderrouladen (German beef rolls)
recipes.description: Thin slices of beef spread with mustard, rolled around onion and gherkin, browned and braised slowly until tender in a dark, glossy gravy. A German Sunday lunch with red cabbage and potato dumplings.

ingredients.name: Beef topside or silverside
ingredients.prep: 4 thin slices (about 180 g each) cut across the grain

ingredients.name: Celery stick (or a chunk of celeriac)
Dry red wine (replace with more stock)

steps.t: Lay the beef slices between cling film and pound them gently to about 5 mm thick, keeping them in one piece. Season one side with salt and pepper and spread each with a tablespoon of mustard, leaving a 1 cm border.

Scatter the sliced onion over the slices, lay a strip of bacon on each if using, and place gherkin strips across the short end. Fold in the long sides by 1 cm, then roll up tightly from the gherkin end and secure each roll with two cocktail sticks or tie with string.

Heat the oil in the casserole over medium-high heat. Brown the rolls on all sides, turning them every minute or so, until deep brown, 8–10 minutes in total. Good colour now gives the gravy its flavour. Lift out onto a plate.

Add the diced onion, carrot and celery to the fat and fry for 5 minutes until browned at the edges. Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute until it darkens to rust red, then pour in the wine if using and scrape up the brown crust from the bottom of the pan.

Add the stock, bay leaves and allspice and return the rolls with their juices. The liquid should come about two-thirds of the way up. Bring to a simmer, cover and braise over low heat for 1½ hours, turning the rolls every 30 minutes, until a skewer slides in with no resistance.
Lift out the rolls and keep them warm. Pour the braising liquid through the sieve into a small pan, pressing the vegetables to push their flavour through, then bring it to the boil.
Stir in the cornflour mixture and simmer for 1–2 minutes until the gravy is glossy and coats the back of a spoon. Taste for salt and pepper.
Remove the sticks or string, return the rolls to the gravy and serve with red cabbage and potato dumplings or boiled potatoes, with plenty of gravy spooned over.

recipes.reheating: Reheat the rolls in their gravy, covered, over low heat until steaming hot throughout.
notes: Rouladen are even better made a day ahead; they freeze well in their gravy for up to 3 months.

recipes.name: Schwäbischer Kartoffelsalat (Swabian potato salad)
recipes.description: Warm sliced potatoes soaked in a hot broth, vinegar and onion dressing until creamy and glossy without any mayonnaise. The classic partner to schnitzel.

ingredients.name: Waxy potatoes (such as Charlotte or Annabelle)

steps.t: Cover the potatoes with cold salted water in the large saucepan, bring to the boil and simmer for 18–22 minutes, until a knife slides in easily but they are not falling apart. Drain and leave until just cool enough to handle.

While the potatoes cook, put the onion, stock, vinegar, mustard, sugar, salt and plenty of pepper in the small saucepan and bring to the boil. Simmer for 1 minute so the onion softens slightly. The dressing should taste quite sharp and salty; the potatoes will absorb a lot of it.

Peel the potatoes while still warm and slice them about 3 mm thick into the bowl. Pour the hot dressing over the warm slices straight away and fold gently with a spatula. Warm potatoes drink up the liquid; cold ones will not.

Leave to stand for 20–30 minutes, folding every 10 minutes, until most of the liquid has been absorbed and the salad looks creamy as the edges of the slices soften into the dressing. Add a few spoonfuls of hot stock if it seems dry.
Fold in the oil and most of the chives, taste and add more salt, pepper or vinegar if needed. Serve lukewarm or at room temperature, scattered with the remaining chives.

recipes.storage: Keeps covered in the fridge for up to 2 days; bring back to room temperature and loosen with a little warm stock before serving.
notes: Swabian cooks traditionally use beef stock; vegetable stock keeps the salad vegan.

recipes.name: Apfelstrudel (Viennese apple strudel)
recipes.description: Paper-thin hand-pulled strudel dough rolled around sliced apples, cinnamon, raisins and butter-toasted breadcrumbs, baked until crisp and dusted with icing sugar.
equipment: Large clean tablecloth or linen sheet

ingredients.name: Strong white bread flour or plain flour
Tart, firm apples (such as Boskoop, Bramley or Granny Smith)
Raisins
ingredients.prep: soaked in warm water for 15 minutes and drained

steps.t: Mix the flour, salt, water, oil and vinegar into a soft dough and knead on the worktop for 8–10 minutes, slapping it down now and then, until it is silky, smooth and elastic and no longer sticks to your hands. Shape into a ball, coat with a little oil, cover with an upturned warm bowl and rest for at least 45 minutes; relaxed gluten is what lets it stretch thin.

Meanwhile melt 60 g of butter in the frying pan over medium heat, add the breadcrumbs and stir for 4–5 minutes until evenly golden and nutty-smelling. Tip onto a plate to cool. Toss the apples with the lemon juice, then mix in the sugar, cinnamon, raisins and walnuts just before you fill the strudel so they don't turn watery.

Heat the oven to 190 °C and line the baking tray with baking paper. Spread the cloth over a table about 1 m long, dust it lightly with flour, and roll the dough out on it into a rectangle as far as the rolling pin will go.

Flour the backs of your hands, slide them under the dough and gently stretch it outwards from the centre, moving around the table, until it is so thin you can read print through it and it hangs over the edges. Small holes don't matter. Cut off the thick rim with scissors.

Brush the dough with about a third of the melted butter. Scatter the toasted crumbs over the third of the dough nearest you, leaving a 5 cm border at the sides, and pile the apple filling on top in a long, even band.

Fold the side borders in over the filling. Lift the edge of the cloth nearest you and let the strudel roll itself up away from you, then roll it from the cloth onto the baking tray, seam side down, curving it into a horseshoe if it is too long. Brush generously with melted butter.

Bake for 35–40 minutes, brushing with the remaining butter twice, until the pastry is deep golden and crisp and juice bubbles at the ends. The apples should be completely soft when pierced through the crust with a thin knife.

Leave to cool on the tray for 15 minutes so the filling sets, then dust thickly with icing sugar and cut into thick slices with a serrated knife. Serve warm with vanilla sauce, lightly whipped cream or vanilla ice cream.

recipes.storage: Keeps at room temperature, loosely covered, for 1 day, or in the fridge for up to 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm slices in a 170 °C oven for 10 minutes to re-crisp the pastry.
notes: If you are short of time, layer 6 sheets of filo pastry, brushing each with butter, instead of pulling the dough; the result is crisper and less tender.

recipes.name: Kaiserschmarrn with plum compote
recipes.description: A thick, fluffy pancake torn into pieces in the pan and caramelised with butter and sugar, served with warm spiced plum compote (Zwetschkenröster). An Alpine hut favourite.
equipment: Large ovenproof non-stick frying pan (28 cm)

steps.t: Make the compote first: put the plums, sugar, water, cinnamon and cloves in the saucepan, cover and simmer gently for 15–20 minutes, stirring now and then, until the plums have collapsed but some halves still hold their shape. Remove the spices and keep warm.
Heat the oven to 180 °C. Whisk the egg yolks, milk, flour, vanilla and salt in a bowl into a smooth, lump-free batter.

In the second, completely clean bowl, whisk the egg whites until foamy, then gradually add the 30 g of sugar and whisk to firm, glossy peaks that stand up when you lift the whisk. Fold the whites into the batter in three additions with a spatula, keeping as much air as possible; a few streaks are fine.

Melt half the butter in the frying pan over medium heat until it foams. Pour in the batter and scatter over the drained raisins. Cook for 3–4 minutes, until the underside is golden and the edges start to set, then transfer the pan to the oven for 6–8 minutes, until the pancake has puffed and the top is set and springs back when touched.
Back on the hob over medium heat, cut the pancake into quarters with a spatula, turn each one over, then tear the pancake into bite-sized pieces with two forks.

Add the remaining butter and the tablespoon of sugar and toss the pieces for 2–3 minutes, until the sugar melts and caramelises and the edges are crisp and glazed. Pile onto warm plates, dust with icing sugar and serve straight away with the warm plum compote.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately. The compote keeps in a jar in the fridge for up to 5 days.
notes: Austrians often soak the raisins in rum; warm water or apple juice keeps it alcohol-free.
Apple sauce or lingonberry jam are other classic partners.

recipes.name: Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte (Black Forest cake)
recipes.description: Three layers of light chocolate sponge filled with thickened sour cherries and vanilla whipped cream, covered in cream and chocolate shavings and crowned with cherries.

steps.t: Heat the oven to 175 °C and line the base of the springform tin with baking paper (don't grease the sides, so the sponge can climb). Sift the flour, cornflour, cocoa and baking powder together twice.

Whisk the eggs and sugar on high speed for 8–10 minutes, until tripled in volume, pale and so thick that a ribbon of batter sits on the surface for a few seconds. This trapped air is the only real raising agent, so don't cut it short.

Sift the flour mixture over the eggs in three batches, folding gently with a large spatula after each until no dry pockets remain. Fold a spoonful of batter into the melted butter, then fold that back into the batter. Pour into the tin and smooth the top.

Bake for 30–35 minutes, until the sponge is risen, springs back when pressed and a skewer comes out clean. Run a knife around the edge, turn out onto a rack and cool completely, ideally for a few hours or overnight, so it slices cleanly.

For the filling, whisk a few spoonfuls of the cherry juice with the cornflour until smooth. Bring the rest of the juice to the boil with the sugar and cinnamon, whisk in the cornflour mixture and boil for 1 minute until thick and clear. Fold in the drained cherries and leave to cool completely.

Whip the cold cream with the icing sugar and vanilla to soft, stable peaks. Stop as soon as it holds its shape; over-whipped cream turns grainy. Cut the sponge horizontally into three even layers with the serrated knife.

Put the bottom layer on a serving plate, spread a thin ring of cream around the edge and fill the centre with the cherry mixture. Cover with a layer of cream about 1 cm thick, then the second sponge, more cream, and the third sponge, pressing it down gently.

Cover the top and sides with most of the remaining cream and smooth it with a palette knife. Pipe 12 rosettes around the top, press the chocolate shavings onto the sides and scatter some on top, and place a cherry on each rosette. Chill for at least 3 hours before cutting with a knife dipped in hot water.

notes: In Germany each sponge layer is sprinkled with a few tablespoons of kirsch (cherry brandy). For an alcohol-free cake, sprinkle with cherry juice instead.
The sponge can be baked a day ahead and wrapped once cool.

recipes.name: Pierogi ruskie (potato and cheese dumplings)
recipes.description: Poland's favourite dumplings: soft half-moons of tender dough filled with mashed potato, tangy curd cheese and fried onion, boiled and served with golden onions in butter and sour cream.

ingredients.name: Twaróg (Polish curd cheese) or well-drained cottage cheese

steps.t: Boil the potatoes in salted water for 18–20 minutes until completely soft. Meanwhile fry the chopped onion in the oil over medium heat for 10 minutes until soft and golden.

Drain the potatoes well and mash or rice them until smooth while hot. Mix in the curd cheese, fried onion with its oil, salt and plenty of pepper. Taste: the filling should be well seasoned and peppery. Leave to cool completely; warm filling makes the dough soft and hard to seal.

For the dough, mix the flour and salt in the bowl, pour in the hot water and oil and stir with a spoon, then knead on a floured surface for 8–10 minutes until smooth, soft and elastic, like an earlobe. Wrap and rest for 30 minutes.

Roll a third of the dough out thinly on a floured surface, about 2 mm thick, keeping the rest covered so it doesn't dry out. Cut out rounds with the cutter. Gather the scraps, cover and re-roll later.

Put a heaped teaspoon of filling in the centre of each round. Fold the dough over into a half-moon and pinch the edges firmly together from one end to the other, pushing out any air. Crimp the edge with your fingers or a fork so the seal holds. Lay the pierogi on a floured tray, not touching, and cover with a cloth.

Bring a large pan of salted water to a gentle boil. Add 12–15 pierogi at a time and stir once so they don't stick to the bottom. When they float, simmer for 2–3 minutes more, until the dough is tender at the crimped edge. Lift out with the slotted spoon.
While they cook, melt the butter in the frying pan and fry the diced onion over medium heat for 8–10 minutes, until deep golden.
Toss the drained pierogi in the onion butter and serve hot with sour cream. Leftovers are excellent fried the next day in a little butter until golden and crisp on both sides.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate cooked pierogi in a covered container for up to 3 days. Freeze uncooked pierogi on a floured tray, then bag them; cook from frozen, adding 2 minutes.
recipes.reheating: Fry in a little butter over medium heat for 3–4 minutes per side until golden and steaming hot.
notes: The name means 'Ruthenian pierogi', after the historical region of Red Ruthenia, now western Ukraine.

recipes.name: Gołąbki (stuffed cabbage rolls in tomato sauce)
recipes.description: Soft white cabbage leaves wrapped around seasoned beef and rice, braised slowly in a tomato sauce until meltingly tender. A Polish family classic, even better the next day.
equipment: Wide flameproof casserole or roasting dish with a lid

steps.t: Bring the very large pot of water to the boil. Lower in the whole cabbage, cored end up, and cook for 3–4 minutes. As the outer leaves turn bright green and pliable, peel them off with tongs and a fork and lift them out. Keep going until you have 12–14 large leaves; chop the small inner heart and set it aside.
Lay the leaves on a board and shave down the thick central rib of each with a small knife so it is as thin as the rest of the leaf. This lets the leaves roll without cracking.
Cook the rice in boiling salted water for 10 minutes, until half-cooked, then drain and cool. Fry the onion in the oil over medium heat for 6–8 minutes until soft and lightly golden.
In the bowl, mix the beef, rice, onion, egg, marjoram, salt and pepper with your hands for a minute until evenly combined and slightly sticky. Divide into 12 portions and shape each into an oval.
Place a portion of filling at the rib end of a leaf, fold the end over it, fold in both sides and roll up firmly into a neat parcel. Repeat with the remaining leaves and filling.

Scatter the chopped cabbage heart over the bottom of the casserole; it stops the rolls catching. Pack the rolls in snugly, seam side down. Mix the tomatoes, tomato paste, stock, sugar and a pinch of salt and pour over, tuck in the bay and allspice; the liquid should almost cover the rolls.
Cover and simmer over low heat, or bake in a 180 °C oven, for 1¼–1½ hours, until the cabbage is very tender and a roll cut in half is cooked through with no pink inside (71 °C in the centre).
If you like, stir a few spoonfuls of hot sauce into the sour cream, then stir it into the sauce around the rolls. Scatter with dill and serve with boiled or mashed potatoes or rye bread.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Polish cooks usually use pork or a pork and beef mix; all-beef keeps the dish halal when made with halal meat.
Freeze the rolls in their sauce for up to 3 months.

recipes.name: Placki ziemniaczane (Polish potato pancakes)
recipes.description: Finely grated potato and onion pancakes, fried until lacy and crisp at the edges and soft in the middle. Eaten with sour cream, sprinkled with sugar or topped with goulash.
equipment: Fine box grater or food processor

steps.t: Grate the potatoes and onion on the fine side of the grater into the bowl (or use the fine grating disc of a food processor). Grating the onion with the potatoes keeps them from turning grey.

Tip the mixture into the sieve over a second bowl and press firmly with a spoon to squeeze out as much liquid as you can. Leave the liquid to stand for 5 minutes, then carefully pour it away, keeping the white potato starch that has settled at the bottom.

Return the potatoes to the bowl with the starch, egg, flour, salt and plenty of pepper and mix well. The batter should be thick and hold together on a spoon; add another spoonful of flour if it is very wet.

Heat about 5 mm of oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat until a drop of batter sizzles immediately. Drop in heaped tablespoons of batter, spaced apart, and flatten each into a thin round about 8 cm across with the back of the spoon.

Fry for 3–4 minutes per side until deep golden brown and crisp, with lacy edges. Drain on kitchen paper and keep warm in a low oven while you fry the rest, adding oil as needed and letting it reheat between batches.
Serve hot, with a spoonful of sour cream and some dill on each portion. For a sweet version, sprinkle with sugar instead; for a hearty dinner, serve topped with goulash (placek po węgiersku).

recipes.storage: Best eaten freshly fried. Leftovers keep in the fridge for 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp on a tray in a 200 °C oven for 8–10 minutes until hot through.
safety: Hot oil spits when wet batter goes in; lower the spoonfuls in gently and keep children away from the pan.

recipes.name: Ukrainian borscht (beet, cabbage and beef soup)
recipes.description: Ukraine's ruby-red national soup: a slow beef broth filled with beetroot, cabbage, potatoes and peppers, sharpened with a little vinegar and finished with garlic, dill and sour cream.

ingredients.name: Beef shin or brisket, ideally on the bone
Raw beetroot
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into thin matchsticks or coarsely grated

steps.t: Put the beef in the pot with the cold water and bring slowly to the boil. Skim off the grey foam with a ladle as it rises for the first 10 minutes so the broth stays clear, then add the bay leaves, allspice and salt, lower the heat and simmer gently, partly covered, for 1½ hours until the beef is tender.
Lift out the beef, cut the meat into bite-sized pieces (discard bone and gristle) and return it to the broth. Add the potatoes and simmer for 10 minutes.

Meanwhile make the zazharka (the fried vegetable base): heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and fry the onion and carrot for 5 minutes until soft. Add the beetroot, vinegar and sugar and cook, stirring, for 8–10 minutes. The acid keeps the beetroot a deep ruby red instead of fading to brown.
Stir in the tomato paste and pepper and cook for 3 more minutes, adding a ladle of broth if the pan looks dry, until the mixture is glossy and smells sweet.

Add the shredded cabbage to the soup and simmer for 5 minutes, then stir in the beetroot mixture. Simmer for another 10 minutes, until the cabbage and beetroot are tender but not mushy and the soup is a deep red.

Stir in the garlic and most of the dill, season with pepper and more salt or vinegar to taste: borscht should be gently sweet-sour. Turn off the heat, cover and leave to stand for 15–20 minutes; the colour and flavour deepen as it rests.
Ladle into bowls and top each with a spoonful of sour cream and the remaining dill. In Ukraine it comes with pampushky (garlic bread rolls), rye bread or a clove of raw garlic.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Every Ukrainian region and family has its own borscht: some add beans, mushrooms or smoked pork; this is a common everyday beef version.
Borscht tastes better on the second day and freezes well for up to 3 months.

recipes.name: Šaltibarščiai (Lithuanian cold beet soup)
recipes.description: A startlingly pink, ice-cold summer soup of kefir, grated beetroot, cucumber, dill and spring onions, served with hot boiled potatoes on the side. Known in Poland as chłodnik litewski.

ingredients.name: Beetroot
ingredients.prep: about 4 medium, scrubbed (or ready-cooked beetroot, not in vinegar)

steps.t: Put the beetroot in the saucepan, cover with water and simmer for 35–40 minutes, until a knife slides easily into the centre. Drain, cool under cold water and rub off the skins with your fingers (wear gloves to avoid pink hands). Skip this step if using ready-cooked beetroot.
Meanwhile, hard-boil the eggs: lower them into boiling water and cook for 10 minutes, then cool in cold water and peel. Chop two of them and halve the other two for the top.

Grate the cooled beetroot coarsely into the bowl. Add the cucumber, spring onions, dill, chopped eggs, lemon juice and salt and mix, then pour in the cold kefir and stir until the soup turns an even, vivid pink. Thin with a little cold water if you prefer a lighter soup.
Taste and adjust with more salt or lemon: it should be tangy, fresh and well seasoned. Chill for at least 30 minutes so the flavours meld; the soup must be served really cold.
Shortly before serving, boil the potatoes in salted water for 18–20 minutes until tender, drain and toss with dill.

Ladle the cold soup into bowls, top each with half an egg and a little extra dill, and serve with a plate of the hot dill potatoes on the side. The contrast of hot potatoes and icy soup is the whole point.

recipes.storage: Keeps covered in the fridge for up to 2 days; stir before serving.
notes: Ready-cooked vacuum-packed beetroot turns this into a 20-minute meal.

recipes.name: Varenyky z kapustoyu (sauerkraut dumplings)
recipes.description: Ukrainian half-moon dumplings in a soft egg-free dough, filled with sauerkraut slowly braised with onion and carrot until sweet and mellow, and smothered in golden fried onions. Traditional on the meatless Christmas Eve table.
equipment: Large frying pan with a lid

ingredients.name: Sauerkraut
ingredients.prep: drained, rinsed if very sour, squeezed dry and chopped

steps.t: Heat 3 tablespoons of oil in the frying pan over medium heat and fry the chopped onions and carrot for 8 minutes until soft and golden. Add the sauerkraut, sugar, pepper, bay leaf and 100 ml water, cover and braise over low heat for 25–30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the cabbage is soft, mellow and the liquid has gone.

Remove the bay leaf and taste: the filling should be gently sour, sweet from the onions and well peppered. Uncover and cook for a few minutes more if it is still moist, then spread on a plate to cool completely. A dry, cold filling makes sealing easy.

For the dough, mix the flour and salt, pour in the warm water and oil, stir and then knead on a floured surface for 8–10 minutes until smooth, soft and elastic. Wrap and rest for 30 minutes so it rolls thin without springing back.

Roll a third of the dough out to about 2 mm thick, keeping the rest covered, and cut out rounds. Put a heaped teaspoon of filling in the centre of each, fold into a half-moon and pinch the edges together firmly from one end to the other, pressing out the air. Crimp or pleat the edge so it holds. Lay on a floured tray under a cloth.

Bring a large pan of salted water to a gentle boil and cook the varenyky in batches of 12–15, stirring once so none stick. When they rise to the surface, simmer for 2–3 minutes more, until the crimped edge is tender.
While they cook, fry the sliced onions in 3 tablespoons of oil over medium heat for 10–12 minutes until deep golden and sweet.
Lift the varenyky out with the slotted spoon, toss with the fried onions and their oil and serve hot, scattered with dill. Outside Lent they are often served with sour cream as well.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate cooked varenyky, covered, for up to 3 days. Freeze uncooked ones on a floured tray, then bag them; cook from frozen, adding 2 minutes.
recipes.reheating: Fry in a little oil over medium heat for 3–4 minutes per side until golden and steaming hot.
notes: Ukrainians make varenyky with potato, cabbage, curd cheese, mushrooms or sour cherries; this sauerkraut version is one of the twelve meatless dishes of Sviata Vecheria.

recipes.name: Chicken Kyiv (kotleta po-kyivsky)
recipes.description: Chicken breasts wrapped around a frozen core of dill and garlic butter, double-crumbed and fried until golden, so the butter bursts out when you cut in.

steps.t: Mash the butter with the dill, parsley, garlic and salt. Spoon it onto cling film, roll into a log about 2 cm thick and freeze for at least 30 minutes until rock hard. A frozen core is what stops the butter escaping during cooking.

Lay each fillet smooth side down and remove the small inner fillet. Cut a deep pocket along the thick side without cutting through, open it out like a book, cover with cling film and pound gently to an even 5 mm. Pound the small fillets thin as well. Season everything with salt and pepper.

Cut the frozen butter into 4 batons. Place one at the narrow end of each opened breast, cover with a small fillet, then fold in the sides and roll up tightly into a neat cigar so the butter is completely enclosed with no gaps.

Set up the flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs in three dishes. Roll each parcel in flour, then egg, then crumbs; then dip again in egg and crumbs for a double coat that seals every seam. Chill on a plate for 30 minutes so the coating sets.
Heat the oven to 180 °C. Heat the oil in the deep pan, no more than one-third full, to 170 °C. Fry two Kyivs at a time for 5–6 minutes, turning gently, until deep golden all over.
Transfer the fried Kyivs to the rack on the baking tray and bake for 10–12 minutes, until the centre reaches 74 °C on a thermometer inserted from the side, avoiding the butter.
Rest for 2–3 minutes, then serve whole with mashed potatoes or chips and green peas. Warn everyone to cut in carefully: the melted butter runs out hot.

recipes.reheating: Reheat on a rack in a 190 °C oven for 15–20 minutes until steaming hot (74 °C) in the middle.
notes: Uncooked, crumbed Kyivs freeze well for up to 2 months; fry from frozen at 160 °C and give them 5 extra minutes in the oven.

recipes.name: Syrniki (farmer's cheese pancakes)
recipes.description: Thick little pancakes made almost entirely of tangy farmer's cheese, bound with an egg and a little flour, fried golden and served with sour cream and jam or berries.

ingredients.name: Tvorog (farmer's cheese), or cottage cheese pressed dry
ingredients.prep: pushed through a sieve if lumpy

steps.t: If you are using cottage cheese, tip it into a sieve lined with kitchen paper, press out as much liquid as you can and leave to drain for 10 minutes. Wet cheese is the main reason syrniki spread and fall apart. Push the cheese through the sieve or mash it well with a fork for a smooth texture.

Mix the cheese with the egg, sugar, vanilla and salt, then stir in the 60 g of flour. The mixture should be soft but hold its shape when scooped; if it is very sticky, add another spoonful of flour, but no more than you need, or the syrniki turn heavy.

Spread the shaping flour on a plate. With wet hands, roll a heaped tablespoon of the mixture into a ball, roll it in the flour and flatten into a patty about 1.5 cm thick and 6 cm across. Neaten the edges with a knife so they are straight; you should get 12.
Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat. Fry the syrniki for 3–4 minutes on the first side until deep golden, then turn carefully with a spatula.
Lower the heat to medium-low, cover the pan and cook for another 3–4 minutes, until the second side is golden and the centres feel springy and are hot right through when one is cut open.
Drain briefly on kitchen paper and serve warm, three per person, with sour cream and berries, jam or a drizzle of honey.

recipes.storage: Keeps in the fridge, covered, for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm in a dry frying pan over low heat, covered, for 3–4 minutes per side.
notes: In Russia and Ukraine the cheese used is tvorog, a dry, crumbly curd cheese; well-drained cottage cheese or Polish twaróg work well.

recipes.name: Svíčková na smetaně (beef in creamy root-vegetable sauce)
recipes.description: The Czech Sunday classic: beef roasted slowly on a bed of carrot, parsley root and celeriac, the vegetables puréed with cream into a sweet-sour sauce, served with sliced bread dumplings, cranberries and a swirl of whipped cream.
equipment: Flameproof roasting dish or casserole with a lid
Large wide pot for the dumplings
Strong thread or a serrated knife

ingredients.name: Beef topside or sirloin, in one piece
Smoked bacon, cut into strips for larding the beef
Plain flour (Czech cooks use coarse 'hrubá' flour)
Cream, whipped with a little sugar

steps.t: Start the dumplings: mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt, add the milk and egg and knead for 8–10 minutes into a smooth, fairly firm, elastic dough. Work in the bread cubes, cover and leave to rise in a warm place for about 1 hour, until doubled.

Heat the oven to 170 °C. Season the beef all over with salt and pepper (if you like, lard it first by threading bacon strips through it with a thin knife). Heat the butter and oil in the roasting dish over medium-high heat and brown the beef on all sides, 8–10 minutes. Lift it out.

Add the onions, carrots, parsley root and celeriac to the fat and fry for 10 minutes, stirring, until golden at the edges. Add the bay leaves, allspice, peppercorns and thyme, pour in the vinegar and stock and return the beef on top of the vegetables.

Cover and roast for 2 hours, turning the beef and basting every 30 minutes, until it is tender when pierced with a skewer and the vegetables are very soft. Add a splash of water if the liquid drops below a third of the way up.

Meanwhile, shape the risen dough into two logs about 6 cm thick, cover and leave for 15 minutes. Bring a wide pot of salted water to a gentle boil, lower in the logs and simmer, covered, for 20 minutes, turning them over halfway, until they sound hollow and spring back when pressed. Lift out, pierce each a few times to release steam and slice with thread or a serrated knife.

Take the beef out, wrap in foil and rest. Fish out the bay leaves, allspice and peppercorns. Whisk the flour into the cream, add it to the vegetables and juices and simmer for 5 minutes, stirring, until thickened.

Blend the sauce until completely smooth and velvety, then push it through the sieve for a fine finish. Season with the mustard, sugar, lemon juice and salt: it should taste creamy, gently sweet and slightly tangy. Thin with a little stock if it is thicker than double cream.

Slice the beef across the grain. Serve each person 2–3 slices with plenty of sauce and 4–5 slices of dumpling, topped with a spoonful of cranberry sauce, a dollop of whipped cream and a slice of lemon, as in every Czech pub.

recipes.reheating: Reheat the beef in the sauce gently, covered, until steaming hot. Steam dumpling slices for 3–4 minutes to refresh them.
notes: Many Czech cooks marinate the beef with the vegetables, spices and vinegar in the fridge overnight before roasting for a deeper flavour.

recipes.name: Bramboráky (Czech garlic and marjoram potato pancakes)
recipes.description: Thin, crisp Czech potato pancakes heavy with garlic and marjoram, fried until brown and lacy and eaten hot from the pan at fairs and pubs.

steps.t: Grate the potatoes finely, tip them into the tea towel and twist it over the sink to wring out as much liquid as possible. Dry potato is what makes bramboráky crisp rather than soggy.

Put the potatoes in the bowl with the garlic, egg, flour, marjoram, caraway, salt and plenty of pepper and mix well. The batter should be thick and loose rather than runny; add a spoonful more flour if liquid pools in the bowl.

Heat about 5 mm of oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat until a little batter sizzles fiercely straight away. Spoon in about 2 tablespoons of batter per pancake and spread it out thinly, about 5 mm thick and 12 cm across; Czech bramboráky are wide and thin.
Fry for 3–4 minutes per side until deep brown with crisp, lacy edges. Drain on kitchen paper and keep warm while you fry the rest, topping up the oil and letting it reheat between batches.
Serve straight away, as they are, with a sprinkle of salt, or with sauerkraut or a cabbage salad. Some Czech pubs also fold them around a spicy stir-fry of meat and peppers.

recipes.storage: Best eaten freshly fried; leftovers keep in the fridge for 1 day.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a hot dry frying pan or a 200 °C oven for 5–6 minutes.
safety: Hot oil spits when wet batter goes in; lower spoonfuls in gently and keep children away from the pan.

recipes.name: Laugenbrezeln (Bavarian soft pretzels)
recipes.description: Chewy, deep mahogany pretzels with a soft crumb and coarse salt, made at home with a baked baking soda bath in place of bakery lye. Best with butter or sweet mustard.
equipment: Large mixing bowl or stand mixer
Two baking trays lined with baking paper

ingredients.name: Coarse pretzel salt or flaky sea salt

steps.t: Bake the baking soda: spread it on a foil-lined baking tray and bake at 120 °C for 1 hour. This turns it into sodium carbonate, a stronger alkali that gives the dark, glossy pretzel crust. Let it cool and store in a jar; handle it with gloves, as it irritates skin.

Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt, add the water and butter and knead for 10 minutes by hand (6–7 in a mixer) into a firm, smooth dough that is barely tacky. Pretzel dough is stiffer than bread dough so the shapes hold. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

Divide into 8 pieces of about 100 g. Roll each into a rope about 60 cm long, thick in the middle (about 2.5 cm) and thin at the ends. Lift the ends, cross them twice to make a twist, then fold the twist down and press the ends onto the thick belly at 4 and 8 o'clock.
Arrange on the lined trays and leave uncovered for 20 minutes, then chill for 20 minutes; a slight skin makes the pretzels easier to dip. Heat the oven to 220 °C.

Wearing gloves, dissolve the baked soda in the water in the stainless-steel pan and bring to a gentle simmer. Lower in one or two pretzels for 20–30 seconds, then lift out with the slotted spoon, let them drip and return them to the paper. They turn yellowish and slippery.
Cut a deep slash across the thick belly of each pretzel and sprinkle with coarse salt. Bake for 14–16 minutes, until deep chestnut brown and the slash has opened into a pale, crisp ridge.
Cool on a rack for 10 minutes and eat the same day, split and spread with butter, or with Weißwurst-style sweet mustard and a radish salad.

recipes.storage: Best on the day of baking. Store leftovers in a paper bag for 1 day, or freeze for up to 1 month.
recipes.reheating: Refresh in a 180 °C oven for 5 minutes.
safety: Baked soda is caustic: wear gloves when handling the powder and the bath, use a stainless-steel pan and keep it away from children.
notes: Bavarian bakers dip pretzels in a 4% food-grade lye (sodium hydroxide) solution; the baked soda bath is a safer home alternative that gives a very similar crust.

recipes.name: Bircher müesli (overnight oats with grated apple)
recipes.description: The original Swiss soaked muesli: oats softened overnight in milk, then stirred with plenty of grated apple, lemon, yogurt and honey and topped with hazelnuts and berries.

steps.t: In the evening, stir the oats into the milk in the bowl, cover and refrigerate overnight (at least 4 hours). The oats absorb the milk and turn soft and creamy without any cooking.

In the morning, grate the apples coarsely, skin and all, straight into the soaked oats, stopping at the core. Add the lemon juice immediately and stir; it keeps the apple from browning and brightens the flavour. Dr Bircher-Benner's original recipe used more apple than oats, so be generous.
Stir in the yogurt and honey until the muesli is loose and creamy. If it is very thick, add a splash of milk; taste and add a little more honey if your apples are tart.
Toast the hazelnuts in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 2–3 minutes, shaking, until fragrant and lightly golden, or use them raw.
Spoon into bowls and top with the berries or fruit and the hazelnuts. Serve chilled, straight away or within a few hours.
To prepare ahead for the week, soak the oats in a lidded container and grate in the apple each morning; the soaked oats keep for 3 days in the fridge.

recipes.storage: Soaked oats keep for 3 days in the fridge; once the apple is added, eat within a day.
notes: Swap half the milk for apple juice for a fruitier, dairy-lighter version.

recipes.name: Beef stroganoff (bef stroganov)
recipes.description: Strips of tender beef seared quickly and folded into a sauce of golden onions, mushrooms, a touch of mustard and plenty of sour cream. A 19th-century St Petersburg classic, ready in half an hour.

ingredients.name: Beef tenderloin or sirloin
ingredients.prep: cut into strips 1 cm thick and 5 cm long

steps.t: Pat the beef strips dry with kitchen paper and season with salt and pepper. Dry meat browns in seconds; wet meat stews and turns grey.

Heat the oil in the frying pan over high heat until it shimmers. Sear the beef in two batches in a single layer for 1–2 minutes, turning once, until browned outside but still pink inside. Tip onto a plate with its juices.

Lower the heat to medium, add the butter and onions and fry for 5 minutes until soft and golden. Add the mushrooms and cook for 4–5 minutes more, until they have released their liquid and it has evaporated and they begin to brown.
Sprinkle over the flour and stir for 1 minute, then pour in the stock and stir in the mustard. Simmer for 1–2 minutes until the sauce thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon.

Turn the heat to low and stir in the sour cream until smooth; don't let it boil or it may split. Return the beef and its juices and warm through for 1–2 minutes, just until the meat is hot but still tender.
Taste for salt and pepper, scatter with dill and serve at once over mashed potatoes, buckwheat or rice, or with crisp potato straws in the Russian style.

recipes.reheating: Reheat gently over low heat, covered, until steaming hot; avoid boiling so the sauce stays smooth.

recipes.name: Pelmeni (Siberian meat dumplings)
recipes.description: Small, thin-skinned dumplings filled with juicy seasoned beef and lamb, folded into little 'ears', boiled with bay leaf and served with butter, sour cream and a splash of vinegar. Made by the hundred and frozen for winter.
equipment: 5–6 cm round cutter or small glass

steps.t: Mix the flour and salt in the bowl, make a well and add the egg, cold water and oil. Stir, then knead on the worktop for 8–10 minutes into a firm, smooth, elastic dough. It should be stiffer than pierogi dough so it can be rolled very thin. Wrap and rest for 30 minutes.

For the filling, mix the beef, lamb, grated onion with its juice, salt and pepper, then add the ice-cold water a little at a time, kneading and slapping the mince against the bowl for 2–3 minutes until it is sticky and holds together. The water makes the filling juicy, almost like soup inside the dumpling.

Roll a quarter of the dough out as thinly as you can, about 1–1.5 mm, keeping the rest covered. Cut out rounds with the cutter. Put a scant teaspoon of filling on each; pelmeni are small, and too much filling tears the dough.

Fold each round in half over the filling and pinch the edge firmly shut into a half-moon. Then bring the two corners together around your fingertip and press them on top of each other, so the dumpling looks like a little ear. Set on a floured tray in a single layer and cover with a cloth.
To freeze, put the trays straight into the freezer for 1–2 hours until hard, then tip the pelmeni into bags. They cook straight from frozen.

Bring a large pan of well-salted water to the boil with the bay leaves. Add the pelmeni, stir once, and when they float, simmer for 4–5 minutes more (6–7 from frozen). Cut one open: the filling should be cooked through with no pink and the dough tender at the joined corners.

Lift them out with the slotted spoon into a warm bowl and toss with the butter. Serve with sour cream, chopped dill and vinegar for sprinkling, or ladle a little of the cooking broth over each bowl as Siberians often do.

recipes.storage: Freeze uncooked pelmeni for up to 3 months. Cooked leftovers keep in the fridge, covered, for 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Fry cooked pelmeni in butter until golden and steaming hot, or warm them in simmering broth.
notes: Classic Siberian pelmeni mix pork and beef, sometimes with lamb or game; this version uses beef and lamb.

recipes.name: Blini (yeasted Russian pancakes)
recipes.description: Thin, lacy, slightly sour yeasted pancakes brushed with melted butter and stacked high, the symbol of Maslenitsa, the Russian Butter Week. Serve with sour cream, honey, jam or smoked salmon.
equipment: 20–22 cm crêpe pan or non-stick frying pan

ingredients.name: Sunflower oil
ingredients.prep: plus a little for the pan

steps.t: Pour half the warm milk into the bowl and whisk in the yeast, sugar and half the flour until smooth. Cover and leave in a warm place for 30–40 minutes, until bubbly and risen. This sponge (opara) gives blini their light texture and gentle sour flavour.
Whisk in the eggs and salt, then the remaining flour, adding the rest of the warm milk gradually so no lumps form. Whisk in the oil. The batter should be the thickness of single cream.
Cover and leave to rise again for 30–40 minutes, until the surface is covered in bubbles. Do not stir it from now on; ladle carefully from the top to keep the bubbles that make the blini lacy.

Heat the pan over medium-high heat and wipe it with a little oil on kitchen paper. Pour in a small ladle of batter and immediately tilt and swirl the pan so it spreads in a thin, even layer. Cook for about 1 minute, until the surface is set and full of holes and the edge is golden and lifting.

Flip the blin with a spatula and cook for 30–40 seconds more, until spotted golden. Slide onto a plate and brush the top with melted butter. Continue with the rest of the batter, stacking the blini and buttering each one; wipe the pan with oil every few blini.
Keep the stack covered with a clean cloth so the blini stay soft. Serve warm, folded into quarters, with sour cream and honey or jam, or with smoked salmon and a little dill for a savoury breakfast.

recipes.storage: Keeps wrapped in the fridge for up to 3 days or frozen for 1 month, interleaved with baking paper.
recipes.reheating: Warm the stack, covered, in a low oven or individually in a dry pan for 20 seconds per side.
notes: The first blin is traditionally a failure ('pervyy blin komom'): it seasons the pan, so don't worry if it tears.

recipes.name: Salat Olivier (Russian potato salad)
recipes.description: The essential New Year's Eve salad: small cubes of potato, carrot, egg, chicken, pickles and peas bound with mayonnaise and dill. Every Russian family has its own version.

ingredients.name: Green peas, canned and drained or frozen and thawed

steps.t: Put the whole potatoes and carrots in a saucepan of cold salted water, bring to the boil and simmer until just tender when pierced with a knife, 15–20 minutes for the carrots and 20–25 for the potatoes. Lift each out as it is done and cool completely. Cutting warm vegetables makes the salad mushy.

Meanwhile, put the chicken and bay leaf in the second pan, cover with cold water, bring to a gentle simmer and poach for 15–18 minutes, until the thickest part reaches 74 °C and the meat is white throughout. Cool in the liquid. Hard-boil the eggs for 10 minutes and cool them in cold water.
Peel the potatoes, carrots and eggs. Cut the potatoes, carrots, eggs, chicken and pickles into small, even dice, about the size of the peas. Neat cubes are the mark of a well-made Olivier.

Put everything in the bowl with the peas, spring onions and most of the dill. Add the mayonnaise, salt and pepper and fold gently until every piece is coated. Taste and add more salt, a splash of pickle brine or a little more mayonnaise if you like.
Cover and chill for at least 1 hour so the flavours come together. Scatter with the rest of the dill before serving, piled in a bowl or pressed into a ring on a plate.

notes: The Soviet classic uses boiled 'doktorskaya' sausage; chicken (as in the Stolichny salad) or boiled beef or beef sausage are common alternatives.
Keep the salad chilled and don't leave it out at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

recipes.name: Shchi with mushrooms (Russian cabbage soup)
recipes.description: Russia's everyday cabbage soup in its Lenten form: white cabbage, potatoes and root vegetables simmered in a broth deepened with fresh and dried mushrooms, tomato and bay, finished with garlic and dill.

ingredients.name: Dried porcini or other dried mushrooms

steps.t: Cover the dried mushrooms with 300 ml of just-boiled water in the small bowl and soak for 20 minutes. Lift them out, chop finely, and strain the soaking liquid through kitchen paper to remove any grit.

Put the rest of the water in the soup pot with the soaking liquid, chopped dried mushrooms, bay leaves and allspice and bring to the boil. Add the potatoes and simmer for 10 minutes, then add the cabbage and simmer for 10 minutes more.

Meanwhile heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and fry the onion, carrot and parsley root for 6–8 minutes until soft and golden. Add the fresh mushrooms and fry for another 6–8 minutes until their liquid has evaporated and they brown at the edges.

Stir the tomato paste and grated tomatoes into the pan and cook for 3–4 minutes, until thick and glossy. Scrape everything into the soup, season with the salt and pepper and simmer for 10 minutes, until the cabbage is soft and silky.
Stir in the garlic and most of the dill, turn off the heat and leave the pot covered for 15 minutes. Shchi always tastes better rested, and better still the next day.
Ladle into bowls and scatter with the remaining dill. Serve with dark rye bread, and a spoonful of sour cream when it is not a fasting day.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: For meat shchi, simmer 600 g of beef brisket in the water for 1½ hours first and use the broth; for sour shchi, replace half the fresh cabbage with sauerkraut.

recipes.name: Grechka s gribami (buckwheat with mushrooms and onions)
recipes.description: Toasted buckwheat cooked until each grain is separate and fluffy, then tossed with mushrooms and onions fried until golden. The comforting, nutty side dish of Russian home cooking.
equipment: Medium saucepan with a tight lid

steps.t: Rinse the buckwheat in the sieve and shake dry. Toast it in the dry saucepan over medium heat, stirring, for 3–4 minutes until it smells nutty and the grains rattle. Toasting keeps the grains separate.

Pour in the water (it will hiss) and add half the salt. Bring to the boil, then cover tightly and cook over the lowest heat for 15 minutes without lifting the lid, until all the water is absorbed and small steam holes appear on the surface.

Meanwhile heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and fry the onions for 6–8 minutes until soft and golden. Turn the heat up, add the mushrooms and the rest of the salt and fry for 7–8 minutes, until the liquid has cooked away and the mushrooms are browned.

Take the buckwheat off the heat and leave it covered for 5 minutes to finish steaming, then fluff with a fork. Fold in the mushrooms and onions, season with pepper, add the butter if using and scatter with dill. Serve with beef stroganoff, meatballs or on its own with a fried egg.

recipes.reheating: Reheat in a covered pan with a splash of water over low heat until hot, or microwave covered.

recipes.name: Medovik (Russian honey cake)
recipes.description: Eight thin, crisp honey layers soaked overnight in a tangy sour cream frosting until they turn soft and cake-like, finished with a coat of golden honey crumbs.
equipment: Heatproof bowl set over a pan of simmering water (bain-marie)
24 cm plate or tart ring as a template
Food processor or rolling pin for crumbs

steps.t: Put the honey, sugar and butter in the heatproof bowl over simmering water and stir until melted and smooth, 4–5 minutes. Whisk in the baking soda: the mixture will foam up and turn a deep amber. Keep whisking for 1 minute, then take the bowl off the heat.

Whisk a few spoonfuls of the warm honey mixture into the beaten eggs, then whisk the eggs into the bowl so they don't scramble. Stir in the flour a third at a time until you have a soft, slightly sticky dough. Divide into 8 equal pieces and keep them covered while warm.

Heat the oven to 180 °C. Roll one piece of dough directly on a sheet of baking paper to a circle a little bigger than 24 cm, about 2 mm thick, dusting with flour as needed. Prick all over with a fork.

Slide the paper onto a tray and bake for 4–5 minutes, until golden brown and set. Immediately lay the plate on top and cut around it with a sharp knife to make a neat circle, keeping the trimmings. Repeat with the remaining pieces, rolling the next layer while the last one bakes.

Bake the trimmings for 2–3 minutes more until crisp, cool, then blitz or crush them into fine crumbs. Whisk the sour cream, condensed milk and vanilla together until smooth; it will be runny, which is what soaks the layers.

Put a layer on a serving plate and spread with about 5 tablespoons of frosting, right to the edge. Continue stacking and spreading, then cover the top and sides with the rest of the frosting and press the crumbs all over.
Cover loosely and refrigerate for at least 8 hours, ideally overnight. The crisp layers absorb the frosting and turn soft and tender. Cut with a sharp knife and serve chilled with tea.

notes: Medovik keeps well for 3 days in the fridge and is at its best on the second day.

recipes.name: Kompot (summer fruit drink)
recipes.description: A light, ruby-coloured drink of fresh fruit and berries simmered briefly in water with a little sugar, then chilled. Served by the jug at every summer meal.

ingredients.name: Cherries (sour or sweet), stoned or whole

steps.t: Bring the water to the boil in the large pot. Add the apples (and lemon zest if using) and simmer for 5 minutes; firm fruit goes in first so it has time to give up its flavour.
Add the cherries and berries, bring back to the boil and simmer gently for 3–5 minutes, just until the berries soften and the water turns deep pink. Longer cooking dulls the fresh flavour.

Stir in the sugar until dissolved, then taste: kompot should be lightly sweet and refreshing, not syrupy. Add more sugar for sour fruit. Turn off the heat, cover and leave to cool completely, so the fruit keeps infusing.
Chill in the fridge for at least 2 hours. Serve cold in glasses, with or without the fruit (many people like to eat it with a spoon), or strain into a jug for a clear drink.

recipes.storage: Keeps in a covered jug in the fridge for up to 4 days.
notes: In winter kompot is made the same way from dried fruit (apples, pears, prunes and raisins), simmered for 20–30 minutes.

recipes.name: Köttbullar (Swedish meatballs with cream gravy)
recipes.description: Small, tender beef meatballs gently spiced with allspice and white pepper, browned in butter and served in a smooth cream gravy with mashed potatoes, lingonberries and quick-pickled cucumber.

steps.t: Stir the breadcrumbs into the milk in the bowl and leave for 10 minutes until soft and pasty. This 'panade' keeps the meatballs tender. Meanwhile soften the onion in 10 g of butter in the small frying pan over low heat for 5 minutes without browning, then cool.

Add the beef, egg, onion, allspice, white pepper and salt to the soaked crumbs and mix with your hands for about a minute until evenly combined; don't overwork it or the meatballs turn dense. Fry a tiny piece to taste for seasoning.
With wet hands, roll the mixture into walnut-sized balls, about 3 cm across; you should get around 30. Lay them on a plate.

Heat the butter and oil in the large frying pan over medium heat until the butter foams. Fry the meatballs in two batches, shaking the pan so they roll around and brown evenly, for 8–10 minutes per batch, until browned all over and cooked through (71 °C in the centre, no pink inside). Keep warm.
Pour off all but about 2 tablespoons of fat. Whisk in the flour over medium heat and cook for 1 minute, scraping up the browned bits, to make a light roux.
Gradually whisk in the stock until smooth, then the cream and soy sauce. Simmer for 3–4 minutes, whisking, until the gravy is smooth and thick enough to coat a spoon. Season with salt and pepper.

Return the meatballs to the gravy and warm through for 2 minutes. Serve with creamy mashed potatoes, a spoonful of lingonberry jam and pressed cucumber, as Swedes do on a Thursday night or at the Christmas julbord.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Swedish home cooks often use half beef and half pork mince; all-beef meatballs are just as common.

recipes.name: Gravlax with mustard-dill sauce (gravlaks, hovmästarsås)
recipes.description: Fresh salmon cured for two days under salt, sugar, white pepper and a blanket of dill until silky and translucent, sliced thin and served with sweet mustard-dill sauce on rye bread or with potatoes.
equipment: Glass or ceramic dish just large enough for the fish
A board and weights (tins or jars)

ingredients.name: Very fresh salmon fillet, skin on, pin-boned
ingredients.prep: sold for raw eating or frozen first (see step 1)

ingredients.name: Fresh dill
ingredients.prep: 1 large bunch, roughly chopped with stalks

steps.t: Unless the salmon is sold for raw eating (already frozen to kill parasites), freeze it in a home freezer (−18 °C or colder) for 7 days to kill any parasites, then thaw it overnight in the fridge. Pat dry and cut the fillet across into two equal halves.

Mix the salt, sugar and crushed white pepper. Sprinkle a quarter of the mix in the dish, lay one piece skin side down on it and cover the flesh with half the remaining cure and all the dill. Sprinkle the rest over the flesh of the second piece and lay it on top, flesh to flesh, thick end over thin end, like a sandwich.

Wrap the dish tightly in cling film, put a board on top and weigh it down with a couple of tins. Refrigerate for 48 hours, turning the salmon parcel over every 12 hours and basting it with the brine that collects. The fish turns firmer and deeper coral as it cures.

Unwrap, scrape off the dill and cure and pat the fillets dry with kitchen paper. Lay them skin side down and, with the long sharp knife held at a low angle, cut very thin slices towards the tail, leaving the skin behind.

For the sauce, whisk the mustard, sugar and vinegar in the bowl, then add the oil in a thin stream, whisking constantly, until thick and glossy like a loose mayonnaise. Stir in the dill and season with a little salt.
Serve the gravlax slices on dark rye bread or crispbread with the sauce, or as a starter with boiled new potatoes, lemon wedges and more dill.

recipes.storage: Keep the cured salmon wrapped in the fridge and eat within 4 days, or freeze slices for up to 1 month.
notes: Many Scandinavians add a splash of aquavit to the cure; it is optional and can be left out.

recipes.name: Smørrebrød (Danish open sandwiches)
recipes.description: Thin slices of dense rye bread spread with butter and piled high with two Danish lunch classics: egg and shrimp (æg og rejer) with lemon and dill, and new potato with mayonnaise, chives and crisp onions (kartoffelmad).

steps.t: Boil the new potatoes in salted water for 12–15 minutes until just tender, then drain and cool completely; they slice neatly only when cold. At the same time, lower the eggs into boiling water and cook for 9 minutes so the yolks are just set, then cool in cold water and peel.
Fry the sliced onion in the oil in the small frying pan over medium heat, stirring often, for 10–12 minutes until deep golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper; they crisp up further as they cool.
Spread every slice of rye bread right to the edges with a thin, even layer of butter. In Denmark the butter is essential: it stops the toppings soaking into the bread.

For the egg and shrimp, lay a lettuce leaf on four of the slices. Slice the eggs and arrange them overlapping on top, then pile the shrimp generously over them. Add a teaspoon of mayonnaise, a lemon wedge and a sprig of dill.

For the potato, spread the remaining four slices with a little mayonnaise. Slice the cold potatoes about 5 mm thick and arrange them in overlapping rows to cover the bread completely. Top with a line of mayonnaise, the radishes, crisp onions and chives, and season with flaky salt and pepper.
Serve on a board with a knife and fork, two pieces per person, eating the fish topping first as Danes traditionally do. Smørrebrød is best assembled no more than an hour before eating.

recipes.storage: Assemble just before serving. Boiled potatoes, eggs and shrimp keep separately in the fridge for 2 days.

recipes.name: Lohikeitto (Finnish creamy salmon soup)
recipes.description: Finland's beloved salmon soup: potatoes, carrot and leek simmered in fish stock with allspice, enriched with cream and finished with chunks of tender salmon and a generous handful of dill.

ingredients.name: Leek (or 1 onion)
ingredients.prep: white and pale green part, sliced

steps.t: Melt the butter in the saucepan over medium heat and add the leek. Cook gently for 4–5 minutes, stirring, until soft and fragrant but not coloured.
Add the potatoes, carrots, fish stock, allspice, bay leaf and salt. Bring to the boil, then cover and simmer for 12–15 minutes, until the potatoes are just tender when pierced with a knife.
Stir in the cream and bring back to a bare simmer. Taste and adjust the salt; the broth should be well seasoned before the salmon goes in.

Lower the salmon into the soup and push it under gently. Keep the heat low, with only an occasional bubble, and poach for 4–5 minutes, until the fish is just opaque all the way through and flakes when pressed. Stir as little as possible so the chunks stay whole.
Take the pan off the heat, fish out the bay leaf and stir in most of the dill and a little white pepper. Leave to stand, covered, for 2–3 minutes for the dill to perfume the soup.
Ladle into warm bowls, scatter with the remaining dill and serve with dark rye bread and butter.

recipes.reheating: Reheat gently over low heat until steaming hot, without boiling, so the salmon stays in pieces.
notes: Some Finnish cooks use milk or a lighter cooking cream; add a spoonful of butter at the end for richness instead.

recipes.name: Kanelbullar (Swedish cinnamon buns)
recipes.description: Soft cardamom-scented buns twisted around a buttery cinnamon filling and topped with pearl sugar, the star of every Swedish fika.
equipment: Large mixing bowl or stand mixer

ingredients.name: Pearl sugar (pärlsocker), or crushed sugar cubes

steps.t: Warm the milk and butter in the saucepan until the butter melts, then cool to lukewarm (about 37 °C, comfortable on your wrist). Hot liquid kills yeast.

Mix the flour, yeast, sugar, cardamom and salt in the bowl, pour in the milk mixture and knead for 8–10 minutes by hand, or 5 in a mixer, into a smooth, soft, elastic dough that comes away from the bowl. Cover and leave in a warm place for about 1 hour, until doubled.
Beat the soft butter, sugar and cinnamon for the filling into a smooth, spreadable paste. Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface and roll it into a rectangle about 30 × 50 cm and 3–4 mm thick.
Spread the filling evenly over the whole surface. Fold the dough in half lengthways to make a long 15 × 50 cm strip, then cut it across into 20 strips about 2.5 cm wide.

Twist each strip a few times, wrap it around two fingers into a knot and tuck the end underneath. Place in paper cases or straight on lined trays, cover with a cloth and leave to rise for 30–40 minutes, until puffy. Heat the oven to 220 °C.

Brush the buns with beaten egg and sprinkle generously with pearl sugar. Bake one tray at a time in the middle of the oven for 8–10 minutes, until deep golden; the bottoms should be lightly browned and the centres springy.
Cool on a rack under a clean tea towel so they stay soft. Serve slightly warm or at room temperature with coffee.

recipes.storage: Keep in an airtight tin for up to 2 days, or freeze for up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Warm frozen buns in a 150 °C oven for 5–8 minutes.
notes: 4 October is Kanelbullens dag, Cinnamon Bun Day, in Sweden.

recipes.name: Kladdkaka (Swedish sticky chocolate cake)
recipes.description: A crisp-topped, deeply chocolatey cake with a gooey, fudgy centre, made in one pan in half an hour. Served with whipped cream and berries.

steps.t: Heat the oven to 175 °C. Butter the springform tin and dust it with the breadcrumbs, tapping out the excess; the crumbs stop the sticky cake gluing itself to the tin.
Melt the butter in the saucepan over low heat, then take it off the heat. Whisk in the sugar, then the eggs one at a time, until glossy. Don't beat in air: kladdkaka should be dense, not fluffy.
Sift in the flour, cocoa and salt, add the vanilla and stir with a spatula just until there are no dry streaks. The batter will be thick and shiny.

Scrape into the tin and smooth the top. Bake for 15–18 minutes, until the top is crisp and slightly cracked and the edges are set, but the middle still wobbles when you shake the tin gently. A skewer in the centre should come out sticky.
Leave to cool in the tin for at least 30 minutes; the centre firms up as it cools into a fudgy layer. For a firmer, truffle-like cake, chill it for 2 hours.
Run a knife around the edge, release the tin and dust with icing sugar. Cut into wedges and serve with softly whipped cream and raspberries.

recipes.storage: Keeps covered at room temperature for 2 days, or in the fridge for up to 4 days.
notes: The gooey centre is part of the charm; bake 3–4 minutes longer if serving to anyone who should avoid undercooked egg.

recipes.name: Fårikål (Norwegian lamb and cabbage stew)
recipes.description: Norway's national dish, made with just four ingredients: layers of lamb on the bone and cabbage wedges with whole black peppercorns and salt, simmered slowly until the meat falls from the bone. An autumn ritual.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a lid (at least 6 litres)

ingredients.name: Lamb shoulder or neck on the bone
ingredients.prep: cut into thick pieces; about a quarter of the weight is bone

ingredients.name: White cabbage
ingredients.prep: 1 large head, cut into 8 wedges through the core

steps.t: Put a layer of lamb pieces, fatty side down, in the bottom of the pot. Cover with a layer of cabbage wedges, then sprinkle with some of the salt, peppercorns and flour. The flour thickens the cooking juices very slightly.
Continue layering lamb and cabbage, seasoning each layer, until everything is in the pot, finishing with cabbage. Press down firmly; the pot will be very full, but the cabbage collapses as it cooks.

Pour in the water, bring to the boil over medium-high heat, then cover, lower the heat and simmer gently for 2–2½ hours. Don't stir; instead, shake the pot now and then and check that there is always some liquid in the bottom, adding a little water if needed.

The fårikål is ready when the lamb is meltingly tender and comes away from the bone easily, and the cabbage is soft, sweet and pale gold from the lamb juices. Taste the broth and add more salt if it needs it.
About 25 minutes before serving, boil the potatoes in salted water until tender, 20 minutes, and drain.

Serve straight from the pot onto warm deep plates: lamb, cabbage and plenty of the peppery broth, with the boiled potatoes and a sprinkle of parsley. Warn guests about the whole peppercorns, or tie them in muslin before cooking.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Fårikål is traditionally eaten on the last Thursday of September, Fårikålens festdag. Like most stews, it is even better reheated the next day.

recipes.name: Plokkfiskur (Icelandic fish and potato stew)
recipes.description: Iceland's thrifty home favourite: flaked cod or haddock and roughly mashed potatoes folded into a peppery, onion-sweet white sauce. Eaten with buttered dark rye bread.

steps.t: Boil the potatoes in their skins in salted water for 20–25 minutes until tender. Drain, peel while warm and cut into rough chunks.

Meanwhile, put the fish in the wide pan, cover with cold salted water and bring just to a simmer. Poach gently for 5–6 minutes, until the flesh is opaque and flakes easily. Lift out, keeping 150 ml of the cooking water, and break into large flakes, removing any bones.
Melt the butter in the heavy saucepan over medium-low heat and cook the onion for 6–8 minutes, stirring, until soft and sweet but not browned.

Stir in the flour and cook for 1–2 minutes to make a roux, then gradually whisk in the warm milk and the reserved fish water. Simmer, whisking, for 3–4 minutes until smooth and thick, like porridge. Season with the salt and pepper.

Add the potatoes and fish and fold together with a wooden spoon, breaking the potatoes up roughly as you go. It should be a chunky, creamy mash, not a purée. Warm through for 2 minutes and taste for seasoning; plokkfiskur should be quite peppery.
Spoon onto plates, scatter with chives and serve with buttered dark rye bread. Some Icelandic cooks top it with grated cheese and grill it briefly until golden.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Plokkfiskur was invented to use up leftover boiled fish and potatoes, so it is a good use of last night's cod.

recipes.name: Ćevapi (Bosnian grilled minced beef fingers)
recipes.description: Small, juicy fingers of seasoned minced beef and lamb, rested overnight and grilled over high heat, then stuffed ten at a time into warm flatbread with raw onion, ajvar and kajmak.
equipment: Barbecue, griddle pan or heavy frying pan
