ingredients.name: Somun or lepinja flatbreads (or large thick pittas)
Kajmak (or cream cheese beaten with a little butter)

steps.t: Put the beef, lamb, garlic, baking soda, salt and pepper in the bowl. Mix and knead with your hands, gradually adding the sparkling water, for 4–5 minutes until the meat becomes sticky and paste-like and comes away from the bowl. The baking soda and kneading give ćevapi their springy, juicy texture.
Cover the bowl tightly and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight, so the flavours develop and the mixture firms up, which makes shaping much easier.
With wet hands, roll the mixture into fingers about 8 cm long and 2 cm thick; you should get about 40. Lay them on a tray without touching. Keep them chilled until the grill is ready.

Heat the barbecue or griddle pan until very hot and brush with oil. Grill the ćevapi in batches for 8–10 minutes, turning every 2 minutes with tongs, until browned and slightly charred all over and cooked through, with no pink in the middle (71 °C).
In the last minutes, warm the flatbreads on the grill, cut side down, so they soak up the meat juices. Split each one open like a pocket.
Fill each bread with ten ćevapi and a generous handful of chopped onion, and add kajmak and ajvar if you like. Serve immediately, with a shopska or cabbage salad and plain yogurt to drink.

recipes.reheating: Reheat in a hot frying pan for 3–4 minutes, turning, until steaming hot throughout.
notes: In Sarajevo ćevapi are made from beef alone, often with a little lamb; Serbian versions often add pork.

recipes.name: Pljeskavica (Serbian grilled patty in lepinja)
recipes.description: A large, thin, juicy patty of seasoned beef and lamb with onion and paprika, grilled hot and folded into warm flatbread with raw onion, tomato, cabbage salad and ajvar. Serbia's favourite street food.
equipment: Barbecue, griddle pan or large heavy frying pan

ingredients.name: Lepinja flatbreads or large thick pittas
Kajmak (or cream cheese beaten with a little butter)

steps.t: Prepare the toppings first: toss the shredded cabbage with a good pinch of salt and a few drops of vinegar and leave it to soften for 15 minutes, then squeeze it lightly. Chop the onion and slice the tomatoes so everything is ready when the meat comes off the grill.

Put the beef, lamb, chopped onion, garlic, paprika, chilli, salt and pepper in the bowl. Knead with your hands for 3–4 minutes, adding the sparkling water a splash at a time, until the mixture is sticky and holds together in one mass. If you have time, cover and chill for 1–2 hours; the patties hold together better.

Divide into 4 portions. Put each between two sheets of baking paper and press out with your palm, then a rolling pin, into a thin patty about 15 cm across and 1 cm thick. Pljeskavica is wide and thin so it cooks fast and stays juicy. Keep chilled until the grill is ready.

Heat the barbecue or griddle pan until very hot and brush with oil. Peel off the paper and grill the patties for 4–5 minutes per side, turning once with a wide spatula, until well browned with charred edges and cooked through (71 °C, no pink in the centre).
While the second side cooks, warm the flatbreads on the grill for a minute and split them open.

Tuck a patty into each bread and pile in chopped onion, tomato slices and salted cabbage, with ajvar and kajmak if you have them. Eat straight away, wrapped in a napkin, with chips or a shopska salad on the side.

recipes.reheating: Reheat in a hot frying pan for 2–3 minutes per side until steaming hot throughout.
notes: For gourmet (punjena) pljeskavica, fold a second thin patty over a filling of kajmak and grated cheese before grilling.

recipes.name: Mici (Romanian garlicky grilled sausages)
recipes.description: Skinless grilled rolls of minced beef and lamb, heavy with garlic and thyme and made springy with baking soda and cold broth. Eaten hot off the grill with plenty of mustard and bread at every Romanian outdoor feast.

steps.t: Put the beef and lamb in the bowl with the garlic, thyme, coriander, allspice, paprika, salt and pepper. Dissolve the baking soda in the cold stock and pour it in gradually while kneading.

Knead the mixture vigorously with your hands for 8–10 minutes, until it turns into a smooth, sticky, almost elastic paste that clings to your fingers. This long kneading, together with the baking soda, gives mici their bouncy, juicy texture.
Cover tightly and refrigerate for at least 12 hours, ideally 24. The baking soda needs time to work and the garlic and thyme flavour deepens.
With wet hands, roll the mixture into sausages about 10 cm long and 2.5 cm thick; you should get 18–20. Keep them on a tray in the fridge until the grill is hot.

Heat the barbecue or griddle pan until very hot and oil the bars. Grill the mici for 10–12 minutes, turning every couple of minutes, until browned and slightly charred outside, juicy inside and cooked through to 71 °C with no pink.
Serve straight from the grill with a generous dollop of mustard and crusty bread, with pickles or a salad of tomatoes and onions alongside.

recipes.reheating: Reheat in a hot frying pan for 3–4 minutes, turning, until steaming hot.
notes: Romanian mici are usually a mix of beef, lamb and pork; this version uses beef and lamb.

recipes.name: Sarma (sour cabbage rolls)
recipes.description: Leaves of whole soured cabbage rolled around beef, rice and paprika, packed into a pot over sauerkraut and simmered slowly for hours until tangy and tender. The centrepiece of winter and holiday tables across the Balkans.
equipment: Large heavy pot (at least 5 litres) with a lid
Small frying pan for the roux

ingredients.name: Whole soured cabbage head (kiseli kupus glavica)
Salt
ingredients.prep: less if the leaves are very salty

ingredients.name: Smoked ribs or smoked bacon, tucked between the rolls

steps.t: Taste a cabbage leaf. If it is very salty or sour, soak the leaves in cold water for 30 minutes, then drain. Shave down the thick central rib of each leaf with a small knife so the leaves roll easily, and tear any very large ones in half.
Heat 3 tablespoons of oil in the frying pan over medium heat and fry the onions for 8 minutes until soft and golden. Take off the heat and stir in the paprika, then cool slightly.
In the bowl, mix the beef, raw rice, onions, pepper and salt with your hands until evenly combined. The rice is added raw: it cooks inside the rolls and swells, so don't overfill.

Place a heaped tablespoon of filling at the rib end of a leaf, fold the end over, roll once, then push the sides in with your finger, or fold them over, and roll up firmly to make a small parcel about 8 cm long.

Spread half the shredded sauerkraut in the bottom of the pot. Pack the rolls in tightly in layers, seam side down, tucking the bay leaves and the smoked meat (if using) in between, and cover with the rest of the sauerkraut. Pour over enough water to just cover the rolls and put a heatproof plate on top to stop them unrolling.

Bring slowly to a simmer, then cover and cook over very low heat for 2½–3 hours, shaking the pot now and then rather than stirring. The sarma is ready when the leaves are very soft and a roll cut open shows tender rice and no pink meat (71 °C).

For the roux, heat 2 tablespoons of oil in the small frying pan, stir in the flour and cook for 2 minutes until light golden. Off the heat stir in the paprika, then whisk in a ladle of the cooking liquid until smooth and pour it over the sarma. Shake the pot to distribute it and simmer for 10 minutes more, until the juices thicken slightly.
Serve hot, 3–4 rolls per person, with some of the sauerkraut and juices, plain yogurt or sour cream and fresh bread or mashed potatoes.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Sarma tastes better reheated the next day, and freezes well in its juices for up to 3 months.
If you can't find whole soured heads, blanch fresh cabbage leaves and add 200 ml of sauerkraut juice to the cooking water.

recipes.name: Burek (Bosnian coiled meat pie)
recipes.description: Thin pastry sheets brushed with oil and rolled around a juicy filling of minced beef and onion, coiled into a round tin and baked until crisp and golden. Bosnia's beloved pita, eaten with a glass of yogurt.
equipment: 30 cm round baking tin or ovenproof pan

ingredients.name: Thin pastry sheets for pita (jufka / kore) or filo pastry

steps.t: Mix the minced beef, onions, salt, pepper, 2 tablespoons of oil and the 60 ml water in the bowl with your hands until evenly blended and soft. The filling goes in raw; the onion juices steam the meat inside the pastry and keep it juicy.
Heat the oven to 200 °C and brush the tin with oil. Keep the pastry under a damp tea towel while you work so it doesn't crack.
Lay two sheets of pastry on the worktop, overlapping slightly if they are small, and brush them lightly with oil. Spread a sixth of the filling in a line along one long edge, about 3 cm wide.
Roll the pastry loosely around the filling into a long tube, rolling away from you. Don't roll too tightly or the burek will split as the meat expands.

Starting in the centre of the tin, coil the tube into a spiral, seam side down. Make the remaining tubes the same way and continue the spiral from the end of the last one, until the tin is filled. Brush the top generously with the remaining oil.
Bake for 40–45 minutes, until deep golden and crisp on top and the filling is cooked through (check the centre with a knife: the juices should be clear and the meat no longer pink).

As soon as it comes out of the oven, sprinkle the burek with the 100 ml of water and cover with the tea towel for 10 minutes. This softens the crust slightly so it cuts without shattering and the layers stay tender.
Cut into wedges and serve warm, with a glass of plain or drinking yogurt, as Bosnians do for breakfast, lunch or a late-night snack.

recipes.reheating: Reheat wedges in a 180 °C oven for 10–15 minutes until crisp and steaming hot in the centre.
notes: In Bosnia only the meat version is called burek; filled with cheese it is sirnica, with spinach zeljanica and with potato krompiruša.

recipes.name: Ajvar (roasted red pepper and aubergine relish)
recipes.description: Sweet red peppers and aubergine roasted until blistered, peeled, chopped and cooked slowly in oil into a thick, smoky, brick-red relish. Made by the crate every autumn and eaten with bread, cheese and grilled meat all winter.
equipment: Two large baking trays or a barbecue
Large bowl and a plate to cover it

ingredients.name: Red peppers (long, fleshy roasting peppers are best)
Hot dried chilli, for a spicy (ljuti) ajvar

steps.t: Roast the whole peppers and aubergine on the trays in a 250 °C oven (or on the barbecue) for 30–40 minutes, turning every 10 minutes, until the skins are blistered and blackened all over and the flesh has collapsed. The aubergine should feel completely soft.

Pile the hot vegetables into the bowl, cover with the plate and leave to steam for 15 minutes; this loosens the skins. Peel the peppers and aubergine, pull out the stems and seeds, and let the flesh drain in a colander for 30 minutes so the ajvar thickens faster.
Chop the flesh very finely with a knife or pulse it in the food processor to a coarse, slightly chunky purée. Traditionally it is minced, not puréed smooth.

Heat half the oil in the wide pot over medium heat, add the pepper mixture and cook, stirring often, for about 1 hour, adding the rest of the oil a little at a time as the mixture absorbs it. Lower the heat as it thickens, because it spits and catches easily; stir from the bottom with the long spoon.

Stir in the vinegar, sugar, salt and garlic (and the chilli, crumbled, if you like it hot) and cook for 10 more minutes. It is ready when it is thick, glossy and darker red, the oil separates at the edges and a spoon drawn through it leaves a clear trail.
Spoon into clean jars, cover the surface with a thin layer of oil and close. Serve at room temperature with bread, white cheese and grilled meats such as ćevapi.

recipes.storage: Keeps in clean jars in the fridge for up to 2 weeks (always use a clean spoon), or freeze in small portions for up to 6 months.
notes: For shelf-stable jars, process the filled jars in a boiling-water bath according to tested home-canning guidance.

recipes.name: Shopska salata (Bulgarian tomato, cucumber and white cheese salad)
recipes.description: Bulgaria's national salad: ripe tomatoes, cucumber, peppers and onion dressed simply with sunflower oil and vinegar, buried under a snowfall of finely grated sirene white cheese.

ingredients.name: Cucumber
ingredients.prep: partly peeled in stripes and diced

ingredients.name: Green or red peppers (roasted and peeled, or raw)
Small red onion, or 4 spring onions

steps.t: Put the tomatoes, cucumber, peppers, onion and most of the parsley in the bowl. If using roasted peppers, char them under a hot grill, steam in a covered bowl for 10 minutes, then peel and slice them first; the smokiness is traditional in summer.
Sprinkle with the salt, pour over the oil and vinegar and toss gently with your hands so the vegetables are coated but the tomatoes stay in chunks. Leave for 5 minutes so the juices start to run.
Divide between plates or pile into a serving bowl. Grate the cold cheese finely over the top in a thick layer, so it covers the vegetables like snow; cold cheese grates much more easily than soft.
Scatter with the rest of the parsley and a slice of hot pepper on top, and serve at once as a starter or with grilled meat and fresh bread. The juices at the bottom of the bowl are for mopping up.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away; undressed vegetables keep in the fridge for a day.
notes: The white, green and red colours echo the Bulgarian flag.

recipes.name: Bulgarian tarator (cold cucumber and yogurt soup)
recipes.description: A chilled summer soup of tangy yogurt thinned with cold water, filled with crunchy cucumber, garlic, dill and toasted walnuts and finished with a thread of sunflower oil. Ready in 15 minutes.

ingredients.name: Plain whole-milk yogurt (Bulgarian if you can find it)
Garlic
ingredients.prep: crushed with a pinch of salt

steps.t: Toast the walnuts in the dry frying pan over medium heat for 2–3 minutes, shaking the pan, until fragrant and lightly golden, then tip onto a plate to cool. Toasting brings out their flavour against the cool yogurt.
Whisk the yogurt in the bowl until smooth, then whisk in the ice-cold water gradually until the soup has the consistency of single cream. Add a little more water if your yogurt is very thick.
Stir in the cucumber, crushed garlic, most of the dill and the salt. Taste: tarator should be tangy, garlicky and quite salty, as it is served very cold, which dulls flavour.
Chill for at least 15 minutes, or up to a few hours, so the garlic and dill infuse the yogurt.

Ladle into bowls, add an ice cube or two on hot days, scatter with the toasted walnuts and the remaining dill and drizzle a little sunflower oil over each bowl. Serve with bread as a starter, or alongside grilled meat or fried courgettes.
If you make it ahead, keep the walnuts separate and add them only at the table so they stay crunchy.

recipes.storage: Keeps covered in the fridge for up to 2 days; stir well before serving.
notes: In North Macedonia and Serbia a similar soup is called taratur or tarator; some cooks leave out the walnuts.

recipes.name: Ciorbă de perișoare (Romanian sour meatball soup)
recipes.description: A clear, gently sour vegetable broth with tender little beef and rice meatballs, tomato and lots of fresh lovage and parsley, finished with lemon. The everyday soup of Romanian home cooking.

ingredients.name: Lemon juice (or 500 ml borș, fermented bran sour)

steps.t: Bring the water to the boil in the soup pot with the chopped onion, carrots, parsley root, celeriac and 1 teaspoon of the salt. Simmer for 15 minutes, until the vegetables are starting to soften.

Meanwhile mix the beef, rice, grated onion, egg, dill, salt and pepper in the bowl until evenly combined. With wet hands, roll into small balls about 2.5 cm across (the size of a walnut); you should get about 30. Wet hands keep the mixture from sticking.

Add the pepper and passata to the soup, then lower the meatballs in one at a time with a spoon. Keep the soup at a gentle simmer rather than a rolling boil, which would break them apart and cloud the broth.
Simmer gently, partly covered, for 25–30 minutes, skimming off any foam, until the meatballs float, are cooked through (71 °C, no pink inside) and the rice in them is completely tender.

Stir in the lemon juice a spoonful at a time and the remaining salt, tasting as you go: ciorbă should be clearly sour but balanced. If you use borș, add it now and bring the soup just back to the boil.
Turn off the heat and stir in the lovage and parsley. Lovage gives the soup its characteristic celery-like aroma, so be generous if you can find it. Leave to stand for 5 minutes.
Serve hot with a spoonful of sour cream, a hot green pepper on the side to bite between spoonfuls and fresh bread, as Romanians do.

recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Romanian cooks often use a mixture of pork and beef mince; all-beef is also common.

recipes.name: Mămăligă cu brânză și smântână (polenta with white cheese, sour cream and fried egg)
recipes.description: Soft, buttery cornmeal porridge piled high with salty crumbled white cheese and cool sour cream, crowned with a fried egg. Romania's beloved peasant breakfast.

ingredients.name: Telemea or brânză de burduf (or feta)

steps.t: Bring the water and salt to the boil in the heavy saucepan. Lower the heat to medium and pour in the cornmeal in a thin, steady rain, whisking constantly so no lumps form.

Switch to the wooden spoon and cook over low heat for 20–25 minutes, stirring every minute or two and scraping the bottom, until the mămăligă is thick and smooth, pulls away from the sides of the pan and the grains no longer taste gritty. Cover the pan between stirs; it spits as it bubbles.

Stir in the butter until melted and glossy. For a soft mămăligă to spoon onto plates, take it off the heat now; for the firm, sliceable version, keep stirring for 5 minutes more and turn it out onto a board.

Shortly before the mămăligă is ready, melt the butter in the frying pan over medium heat and fry the eggs for 3–4 minutes, until the whites are completely set and the edges lightly crisp, leaving the yolks runny or cooking them through as you prefer.
Spoon the hot mămăligă onto warm plates, scatter thickly with crumbled cheese, add a generous spoonful of sour cream and top with a fried egg and a grind of black pepper.
Serve at once, while the cheese is just starting to melt into the porridge. Leftover firm mămăligă can be sliced and fried in butter the next day.

recipes.reheating: Slice cold mămăligă and fry in butter for 3–4 minutes per side, or loosen with a splash of water over low heat until hot.
notes: For mămăligă cu brânză without the egg, it is a classic side for sarmale and tochitură.

recipes.name: Tavče gravče (Macedonian baked beans)
recipes.description: North Macedonia's national dish: large white beans simmered until creamy, then baked in a clay dish with sweet fried onions, paprika, dried red peppers and mint until a golden crust forms on top.
equipment: Shallow clay or ceramic baking dish (tava), about 25 cm

ingredients.name: Dried large white beans (tetovac or butter beans)

steps.t: Drain the soaked beans, put them in the saucepan, cover with fresh water and bring to the boil. Boil for 10 minutes, then drain and cover again with fresh hot water by 3 cm. Changing the first water is a Macedonian habit that makes the beans easier to digest.

Add the bay leaves and simmer gently, partly covered, for 60–80 minutes, until the beans are completely tender and creamy inside but still whole. Add salt only in the last 15 minutes, as early salt can toughen the skins. Keep plenty of liquid: the beans should stay covered.

Meanwhile heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and fry the onions for 10–12 minutes, stirring, until soft and golden. Stir in the flour and cook for 1 minute, then take the pan off the heat and stir in the paprika so it colours the oil without burning.

Heat the oven to 200 °C. Stir the onion mixture, mint and pepper into the beans and their liquid and simmer for 5 minutes. The mixture should be loose and soupy at this stage; it thickens a lot in the oven.

Pour into the baking dish and press the dried peppers into the surface. Bake for 40–45 minutes, until most of the liquid has been absorbed, the edges are bubbling and the top has a golden, slightly crisp crust.
Leave to rest for 10 minutes, sprinkle with parsley and serve straight from the dish with crusty bread, pickled peppers and a cabbage or tomato salad.

recipes.reheating: Reheat in a 180 °C oven, or covered over low heat with a splash of water, until steaming hot.
notes: Tavče gravče is a traditional fasting dish; for a non-fasting version, bake it with slices of beef sausage pressed into the top.

recipes.name: Gibanica (Serbian cheese and egg filo pie)
recipes.description: Layers of crumpled filo soaked in a mixture of eggs, yogurt and two white cheeses, baked until puffed, golden and custardy. Serbia's favourite breakfast and holiday pie.

ingredients.name: White brined cheese (feta or Serbian sir)
Cottage cheese or fresh curd cheese

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200 °C and brush the baking dish generously with oil. Keep the filo under a damp tea towel while you work.

Whisk the eggs in the bowl, then whisk in the yogurt, sparkling water, oil, baking powder and salt. Stir in the crumbled white cheese and the cottage cheese. The mixture will be lumpy and quite runny; that is what makes the pie moist.
Lay two sheets of filo in the base of the dish, letting them come up the sides, and spoon over a little of the egg and cheese mixture.

Take one sheet at a time, dip or brush it all over with the cheese mixture, then crumple it loosely like a ruffled scarf and lay it in the dish. Continue, packing the crumpled sheets in loosely side by side, until all but two sheets are used. The air pockets between the ruffles are what make gibanica light.
Cover with the last two sheets, folding in the overhanging edges, and pour the remaining mixture over the top, letting it seep down between the layers. Brush the top with a little oil.
Bake for 35–40 minutes, until well puffed and deep golden, and a knife pushed into the centre comes out without wet egg.
Leave to rest for 10 minutes; it will sink slightly as it sets. Cut into squares and serve warm or at room temperature, with a glass of yogurt or kefir for breakfast.

recipes.storage: Keeps covered in the fridge for up to 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm squares in a 180 °C oven for 10 minutes until hot through.
notes: Gibanica is always on the table for Serbian Christmas and Easter breakfasts and family celebrations (slava).
